title: Evacuation to Backfill Procedures: Node GPU Replacement & Capacity Burst (Draft)
content:
Purpose:
This is a working draft runbook for handling node-level GPU hardware failures, safe evacuation/drain of pods, orchestrated capacity backfill (burst), and coordinated cluster recovery. The intent is to capture pragmatic steps that on-call SREs can follow during an incident that impacts GPU-backed inference capacity, and to document automated helpers and manual fallbacks.

Scope / When to use this runbook:
- A physical GPU failure is detected (hardware alerts, ECC errors, GPU OOMs, PCIe comms faults).
- Multiple nodes are becoming degraded and scheduler performance/queues are backing up.
- Automated scaling cannot meet latency SLOs and we need emergency capacity injection or node replacement.

Important notes (draft):
- This document intentionally mixes automated procedures and manual operator fallbacks. Keep calm, do not run destructive commands without confirmation from a secondary on-call.
- TODO: add exact Terraform/GCP/AWS CLI snippets for our current fleet; this draft uses examples and placeholders.

Initial Triage (first 10 minutes):
1) Identify the scope: check monitoring dashboards (GPU-error-rate, node-health, pod-evictions, queue-latency). Collect cluster and node names affected.
2) Open/annotate an incident in JIRA/JAM: link alerts and capture the hypothesis. Tag as "inference-capacity".
3) Post to #sre-oncall and #infra-ops Slack channels with short summary and affected models/pools. Example message: "INCIDENT: node n-gpu-17 showing ECC+PCIe faults, 2 pods OOM, inference latency > SLO for dedicated-pool-3. Starting evacuation."
4) Assign roles: primary on-call (executes runbook), secondary on-call (reviews actions, communications), hardware-ops (coordinates physical swap / remote hands), product-impact lead (customer comms).

Safe Evacuation / Cordon + Drain flow:
Goal: move inference workloads off the failing node(s) with minimal cache loss and SLO impact.
Pre-steps: ensure autoscaler is enabled for target pools and that backfill pool has capacity or can be provisioned.

Commands (k8s examples):
- kubectl cordon NODE_NAME  # prevents new pods from scheduling
- kubectl get pods --field-selector spec.nodeName=NODE_NAME -o name  # list pods to evict
- kubectl drain NODE_NAME --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120 --timeout=10m  # gentle drain with 2 minute grace for inference containers

Drain considerations specific to GPU inference: 
- KV caches and prefix caches live in-memory; draining leads to cache re-warm. Prefer draining replicas in a staged fashion to avoid full cache churn.
- If pods use local SSD for ephemeral cache, ensure --delete-local-data only used when unavoidable. Documented local volumes: /var/lib/redwood/cache.
- If a node hosts long-running pinned sessions, coordinate with the product lead to gracefully migrate sessions using the session handoff endpoint (/admin/sessions/hand_off).

Staged evacuation pattern (recommended):
1) If multiple nodes unhealthy, select lowest-util node to evacuate first.
2) Cordon node. 3) Drain with 120s grace. 4) Monitor rollout: check model latency for impacted routes for 5 minutes.
5) If errors or latency spike, pause further drains and open a decision call.

If drain fails (pods stuck Terminating):
- kubectl describe pod POD -n NAMESPACE to see stuck finalizers
- kubectl get events -n NAMESPACE | grep POD_NAME
- If pod is stuck on local volume delete, coordinate with platform-engineering for forced delete: kubectl delete pod POD --grace-period=0 --force (last resort)

Physical GPU replacement path (hardware ops):
1) Verify warranty/remote-hands process and open hardware ticket with provider.
2) If remote-hands is scheduled, ensure node remains cordoned.
3) If immediate physical swap is required to restore capacity quickly, confirm a maintenance window with product-impact lead if customer-facing latency is affected.
4) Post-swap: node needs BIOS/driver verification. Commands to check driver/gpu state (example): 
   - nvidia-smi -q | grep -E "(Driver Version|Product Name|Serial Number)"
   - dmesg | grep -i nvidia
5) Reboot node into maintenance kernel, validate GPU shows expected memory and PCIe link.
6) Uncordon node when healthy: kubectl uncordon NODE_NAME

Emergency Capacity Backfill (burst) 
Use-case: cluster has lost capacity and autoscaler cannot immediately provision enough replacements because of limits or image bootstrap time.
Automated path (preferred):
- Trigger auto-backfill tool: /ops/auto-backfill --pool=dedicated-pool-3 --count=3 --reason="hardware-failure-evac"
- Monitor boot logs in the auto-backfill dashboard and ensure kubelet registers.
Manual path (fallback):
- For cloud: aws ec2 run-instances --launch-template lt-XXX --count 3 --instance-type p4d.24xlarge (replace with our GPU SKU)
- For metal/colocated: create new machine via provisioning portal and tag for k8s cluster join; coordinate remote-hands.
- After node boots, verify node labels and taints (gpu=true, inference=true) and that it's accepted by cluster autoscaler.

Capacity validation checklist:
- New node appears in kubectl get nodes and shows Ready.
- kubectl describe node NODE | grep -i allocatable to confirm GPU resources present.
- Run small smoke test invoking a cheap model route to validate inference path.
- Monitor redis/kv cache hit rates for the pool — expect temporary degradation.

Cluster recovery after multi-node loss:
- If >10% of GPU capacity lost or scheduler behaves badly, consider activating degraded-mode routing: route non-critical traffic to lower-tier models or host in a different region. Documented flag: routing.enable_degraded_mode = true in the console.
- For persistent control-plane issues, escalate to platform-engineering: run control-plane-health diagnostics: etcd health, api-server latency, kube-scheduler queue length.
- If etcd quorum lost, follow the control-plane recovery runbook (link: CONFLUENCE-DB-RECOVERY).

Rollback criteria / Abort plan:
- If after node uncordon we observe repeated GPU errors, immediately cordon again and open a hardware investigation.
- If backfilled nodes are failing to register or causing latency regressions, drain them and stop the auto-backfill process; revert routing to pre-incident model traffic split.

Post-incident validation and follow-up (postmortem steps):
1) Create an incident postmortem within 72 hours. Include timeline of actions, decision points, metrics (latency, errors, capacity before/after), and root cause hypothesis.
2) Action items: update automation scripts to include graceful session handoff endpoint in drain flows; add node-level health checks to detect GPU pre-failure earlier; add runbook sections for forced-deletion safe checks.
3) Run a tabletop test for evacuation/backfill at least once per quarter.

Communications (short template):
- Slack: #sre-oncall initial; #product-updates for customer-facing impact; #infra-ops for hardware timeline.
- Customer status page: use template "We are investigating increased inference latency for Dedicated Pool X; mitigation in progress."

Known limitations & TODOs (draft):
- TODO: add provider-specific CLI snippets (GCP, AWS) copied from infra repo.
- TODO: define exact warm-up strategy for KV caches and expected hit-rate curves post-evac.
- TODO: include runbook checklist for air-gapped/private deployments (private plane: on-prem steps differ—need separate section).
- Known issue: draining large pinned-session pods can take >10 minutes; need flow for session-preserving handoff.

Metrics to capture for post-incident review (for observability):
- pre/post capacity (GPU count), scheduler pending pods, per-route p95 latency, token cost delta, kernel errors on nvidia-smi, number of forced deletes.

Appendix (quick commands & links):
- kubectl cordon/uncordon/drain commands (see above)
- Auto-backfill service: github.com/redwood-inference/infra/auto-backfill
- Incident template: CONFLUENCE-SRE/incident-template
- Slack channels: #sre-oncall, #infra-ops, #product-updates

Draft sign-off: Aisha Patel (SRE lead), review by Michael Chen and Ellen Rivera.

Document status: draft — intended for review. This version emphasizes minimizing cache churn, staged drains, and prioritizing automated backfill while providing manual fallbacks and hardware coordination notes.
